description: Prior Driven Uncertainty Approximation attacks generate adversarial examples by leveraging prior knowledge about input distributions and model uncertainty, even when the model is a black box. The attack perturbs inputs in a way that maximizes uncertainty or misclassification likelihood, often using random search guided by priors.
mechanism: 1. The attacker estimates input priors and uncertainty regions using available data or surrogate models. 2. Random perturbations are applied to inputs, guided by these priors to increase the chance of causing model uncertainty or misclassification. 3. The attacker queries the black-box model to observe outputs and iteratively refines perturbations. 4. The process continues until a perceptually similar adversarial example is found.
defence_mechanism: A-PD-UAP (Adversarial Prior-Driven Universal Adversarial Perturbations) and adversarial training defend by exposing the model to similar uncertainty-driven or universal perturbations during training, increasing robustness to such attacks by reducing sensitivity to these perturbations.
variants: Universal Adversarial Perturbations, Query-based Black-Box Attacks, Randomized Smoothing Attacks
threat_model: black-box; attacker can query the model and has access to input data distribution or priors, but not model internals or gradients
target_vulnerability: The attack exploits the model's sensitivity to input uncertainty and its inability to generalize well to perturbed inputs outside the training distribution.

description: The Network For Adversary Generation (NAG) attack uses a neural network to generate adversarial examples that fool a target model, even when the model's internal details are unknown.
mechanism: 1. Train a generator network to produce perturbations that, when added to input data, cause misclassification by the target model. 2. Use random perturbation search to explore the space of possible adversarial examples. 3. Query the black-box model with perturbed inputs and use the feedback to update the generator. 4. Iterate until successful adversarial examples are found.
defence_mechanism: A-NAG/Adversarial Training counters this attack by augmenting the training data with adversarial examples, including those generated by NAG, thereby improving the model's robustness to such perturbations.
variants: None well-known
threat_model: black-box; attacker can query the model and observe outputs but does not have access to model parameters or architecture
target_vulnerability: Susceptibility of the model to input perturbations that are imperceptible to humans but cause misclassification

These perturbations are iteratively adjusted to maximize the misclassification or detection failure rate across many images. 3. The process continues until a universal perturbation is found that reliably degrades model performance. 4. The final perturbation is applied to new images to induce errors in the target model.

variants: UAP (Universal Adversarial Perturbations), Patch Attacks, None well-known
threat_model: black-box; attacker does not require access to model internals or gradients, only the ability to query the model and observe outputs

Perturbations are optimized using random search to maximize misclassification across a dataset, guided by cosine similarity between feature representations. 3. The crafted perturbation is applied to all inputs, causing consistent misclassification. 4. The process is repeated iteratively to improve attack effectiveness.

variants: Jigsaw-UAP, Cos-UAP, Patch-based UAP, None well-known

defence: Diffusion Process Consistency Checks / Trigger Image Detection / Backdoor Input Filtering / Model Fine / Reverse Engineering and Visualization / Diffusion Step Randomization / Ensemble Defenses
description: TrojDiff_Backdoor_Attack embeds a hidden trigger pattern into training data so that a diffusion model generates attacker-chosen outputs when the trigger is present, while behaving normally otherwise.
mechanism: 1. The attacker crafts or selects a trigger pattern and injects it into a subset of training images. 2. These poisoned images are labeled with attacker-chosen target outputs. 3. The diffusion model is trained on the mixed clean and poisoned data, learning to associate the trigger with the target output. 4. At inference, presenting the trigger causes the model to generate the attacker's desired output.

target_vulnerability: Susceptibility of diffusion models to learn spurious correlations between trigger patterns and outputs during training

defence: Frequency / Spread / Robustness verification / Ensemble watermarking / Model fingerprinting via activation patterns / Adversarial training / Integrity verification
description: A Frequency-based Removal Attack targets and removes or perturbs data samples that occur with high frequency in the training set, aiming to degrade model performance by eliminating representative or influential examples.
mechanism: 1. The attacker identifies high-frequency or commonly occurring samples in the training data (e.g., via access to data statistics or surrogate queries). 2. These samples are selectively removed or perturbed, reducing their influence on the model's learning process. 3. The model is retrained or updated on the manipulated dataset, leading to degraded accuracy or biased predictions.
defence_mechanism: Frequency and spread analysis can detect abnormal reductions in common samples; robustness verification checks model stability to data removal; ensemble watermarking and model fingerprinting can reveal tampering via unexpected activation patterns; adversarial training increases resilience to such manipulations; integrity verification ensures dataset completeness and authenticity.
variants: Influential instance removal, Label flipping on frequent samples, Targeted data subset removal

description: The Spill Over attack injects crafted data points near the boundary of clusters in K-Means, causing the cluster centroids to shift and misclassify legitimate samples.
mechanism: 1. The attacker identifies the boundary region between two or more clusters. 2. Randomly generates and injects data points (poisoning samples) near these boundaries. 3. During K-Means training, these points pull the centroids toward the boundary, distorting cluster assignments. 4. As a result, legitimate data points may be assigned to incorrect clusters.
defence_mechanism: Spill Over Attack/Preprocessing detects and removes or downweights suspicious points near cluster boundaries before clustering, reducing the influence of poisoned samples on centroid positions.
variants: Centroid Poisoning, Boundary Attack, None well-known
threat_model: grey-box; attacker knows the clustering algorithm and can inject data into the training set but may not know the exact data distribution
target_vulnerability: Sensitivity of K-Means centroids to outliers and boundary points

description: This attack manipulates the clustering outcome of K-Means by exploiting the non-convexity of its optimization, introducing small, perceptually similar perturbations to data points to steer cluster assignments.
mechanism: 1. The attacker computes gradients of the K-Means objective with respect to input data points. 2. Using a Lipschitz-constrained gradient search, the attacker perturbs selected points within perceptual bounds. 3. These perturbations are crafted to push the K-Means algorithm toward poor local minima, resulting in incorrect or misleading clusters.
defence_mechanism: NonConvex Optimization/Non-convex Guarantee defences aim to provide robustness by ensuring the optimization process avoids poor local minima, either through robust initialization, regularization, or theoretical guarantees that limit the impact of adversarial perturbations on clustering outcomes.
variants: Adversarial Clustering, Poisoning K-Means, Cluster Membership Attacks
threat_model: white-box; attacker requires access to the model, data, and clustering algorithm internals to compute gradients and craft perturbations
target_vulnerability: The attack exploits the non-convexity of the K-Means objective, which allows small input changes to cause large shifts in cluster assignments.

description: Poisson-Gaussian Noise attacks add a combination of Poisson (signal-dependent) and Gaussian (signal-independent) noise to input data, degrading model performance by mimicking realistic sensor noise.
mechanism: 1. The attacker samples Poisson noise based on the pixel intensity of the input (signal-dependent). 2. Independently, Gaussian noise is sampled and added to each pixel (signal-independent). 3. The combined noise is added to the original input, producing a perturbed sample. 4. The perturbed input is fed to the Gaussian Mixture (GM) model to induce misclassification or degrade accuracy.
defence_mechanism: M-Gaussian Noise/Preprocessing reduces the effect of input noise by denoising or smoothing, while Certified Robustness provides formal guarantees that the model's predictions remain stable under bounded noise perturbations.
variants: Pure Gaussian Noise Attack, Pure Poisson Noise Attack, Salt-and-Pepper Noise Attack
threat_model: black-box; attacker only needs access to the input data and does not require knowledge of model parameters or architecture
target_vulnerability: Exploits the model's sensitivity to input noise and lack of robustness to realistic sensor perturbations

description: UBAC (Unnoticeable Boundary Attack on Clustering) subtly perturbs input data to manipulate DBSCAN clustering results without perceptible changes. The attack aims to shift data points across cluster boundaries, causing misclustering.
mechanism: 1. Identify data points near DBSCAN cluster boundaries. 2. Apply small, random perturbations to these points within perceptual limits. 3. Evaluate if perturbed points cross density thresholds, altering cluster assignments. 4. Iterate to maximize misclustering while maintaining imperceptibility.
defence_mechanism: M-DBSCAN and DBSCAN Preprocessing Sanitizing detect and remove or correct outlier or suspicious points before clustering, reducing the impact of adversarially perturbed samples on cluster formation.
variants: Boundary Attack on Clustering, Adversarial Clustering Attacks, None well-known
threat_model: grey-box; attacker knows DBSCAN parameters and has access to input data but not model internals
target_vulnerability: Sensitivity of DBSCAN to small changes near cluster boundaries and reliance on local density for cluster assignment

mechanism: 1. The attacker selects input samples and applies small, random perturbations that are perceptually similar to legitimate data. 2. These poisoned samples are injected into the training dataset. 3. The clustering algorithm (CA) processes the mixed dataset, causing subtle shifts in cluster boundaries or assignments. 4. The attack aims to maximize impact while minimizing perceptual and statistical detectability.
defence_mechanism: DBSCAN Preprocessing Sanitizing detects and removes outlier or low-density points before clustering, which helps eliminate stealthy poisoned samples that do not conform to the main data distribution, thereby mitigating the attack's effect.
variants: Clean-label poisoning, Backdoor attacks, None well-known
threat_model: grey-box; attacker can inject data into the training set and has partial knowledge of the data distribution and clustering process
target_vulnerability: Susceptibility of clustering algorithms to small, imperceptible data perturbations that can disproportionately affect cluster structure

description: The FNR attack aims to increase the false negative rate of a classifier by injecting adversarial samples that are misclassified as benign. Attackers randomly perturb data to evade detection by the model.
mechanism: 1. The attacker selects or generates malicious samples. 2. Random perturbations are applied to these samples to make them resemble benign data. 3. The perturbed samples are injected into the training or test set. 4. The model is fooled into misclassifying these adversarial samples as benign, increasing the false negative rate.
defence_mechanism: A-Weak Long Attacks/DBSCAN Preprocessing Sanitizing detects and removes outlier or clustered suspicious samples before training or inference, reducing the impact of randomly perturbed adversarial data by filtering out points that do not conform to the expected data distribution.
variants: Label flipping, Clean-label poisoning, Back-gradient poisoning
threat_model: grey-box; attacker has partial knowledge of the model or training data and can inject or modify samples
target_vulnerability: Susceptibility to data distribution shifts and inability to distinguish adversarially perturbed samples from genuine benign data

description: The FNR-Boiling Frog-PA attack gradually injects poisoned data points into the training set to increase the model's false negative rate (FNR) without triggering obvious detection.
mechanism: 1. The attacker randomly selects and perturbs data points to craft poison samples that are close to the decision boundary. 2. These poisoned samples are incrementally injected into the training data over multiple rounds, mimicking a 'boiling frog' effect to avoid abrupt distribution shifts. 3. The model is retrained after each injection, slowly shifting the decision boundary to misclassify more positive instances as negative. 4. The process continues until the desired FNR is achieved or detection risk increases.
defence_mechanism: DBSCAN Preprocessing Sanitizing clusters the training data and removes or downweights outliers and small clusters, which are likely to contain poisoned points, thereby mitigating the gradual accumulation of adversarial samples.
variants: Boiling Frog Attack, Incremental Poisoning, None well-known
threat_model: grey-box; attacker can inject data into the training set and may have partial knowledge of the model or training process
target_vulnerability: Susceptibility to gradual distribution shifts and reliance on training data integrity

The clustering algorithm (CA) is retrained on the poisoned data, causing misclassification or altered cluster boundaries. 4. The attacker observes the impact and may iterate to refine the attack.
